html:
In October 2017 a decree of President Nursultan Nazarbayev ordered Kazakhstan to switch the Kazakh language from the Cyrillic script to a Latin alphabet. The first target date was 2025; it was later moved to 2031.

Kazakh has been written in several scripts over time. It used the Arabic script before Soviet rule, a Latin alphabet from 1929, and Cyrillic from 1940, a choice that tied it closely to Russian. Kazakhs in China, Iran and Afghanistan still use Arabic letters.

The change is about identity and direction. A Latin script brings Kazakh closer to Turkish and the other Turkic languages, and to English, and steps away from Moscow without breaking with it. The first version of the new alphabet, with many apostrophes, was mocked and soon revised. Uzbekistan made a similar switch in 1993, and has found it slow to finish.
